headline_en: 12 Bangladeshi migration hopefuls die in Libya; case filed against 4 brokers in Sunamganj
summary_en: A short text accompanying a video report (published 31 March 2026). It says a case has been filed at Dirai police station in Sunamganj against a broker ring over the deaths of 12 young men in the Mediterranean while going from Libya to Greece, allegedly from lack of food and water. The headline says the case is against 4 brokers; no names or other details are given in the text.

facts.statement: 12 young Bangladeshi men seeking to migrate died in the Mediterranean Sea while travelling from Libya to Greece; it is alleged they died from lack of food and water (reported 31 March 2026).
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo video report text (allegation, source not named)

facts.statement: A case was filed at Dirai police station (Dirai Thana), Sunamganj, against a broker ring over the deaths of 12 young men in the Mediterranean on the Libya-to-Greece route; the headline says the case is against 4 brokers (reported 31 March 2026). The brokers are not named.
The 12 Bangladeshi men who died were travelling by sea from Libya to Greece across the Mediterranean, arranged by a broker ring based in Sunamganj (reported 31 March 2026).

headline_en: In the Saudi crisis, how prepared is the state for expatriate Bangladeshis in danger?
summary_en: Opinion column (21 October 2026) by Dr Selim Reza of North South University's Centre for Migration Studies on the ongoing Saudi crisis: labour-market trouble, attacks or security risk at airports, cancelled flights, visa uncertainty and stranded workers. He describes who is hit by flight disruption and what they risk, and lists what the government should do: verified information, separate lists and a database of affected workers, hotlines and help desks, negotiation with Saudi authorities on visa and job extensions, free rebooking and refunds, loan relief, and a permanent emergency protection fund. It contains recommendations, not announced measures.

facts.statement: The column describes a current crisis for Bangladeshi workers in Saudi Arabia made up of labour-market trouble, attacks or security risk at airports, flight cancellations, visa uncertainty and workers being stranded.
facts.source_in_article: Columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

facts.statement: Saudi Arabia is described as one of Bangladesh's most important labour markets, with very large numbers of Bangladeshis working in construction, transport, cleaning, domestic work and other sectors.

When flights are disrupted by war or security risk, three groups are hit hardest: workers who came home to Bangladesh on leave, workers travelling to join a new job, and people stuck abroad. The risks listed are loss of ticket money, missing the deadline to join the job, losing the job, visa expiry, higher housing and food costs, and loss of income.

The columnist warns that without a coordinated information system between embassies, consulates, airlines, the expatriates' welfare ministry and other authorities (which airports are open, which routes have flights, who is stuck where), people will rely on rumours, fall into brokers' traps, or run from office to office.

The columnist recommends the government make separate lists of (1) workers stranded in Saudi Arabia, (2) workers who returned to Bangladesh and cannot get back to their workplace, and (3) newly recruited workers waiting to travel, recording their location, visa validity, job contract, employer identity, unpaid wages and debts in a combined digital database shared between the embassy, the ministry, BMET (Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training), airlines and recruiting firms.

The columnist recommends that at the start of a crisis a multilingual hotline, online registration and an emergency help desk be activated, and that stranded workers get food, safe housing, medical and legal help; those needing repatriation should be returned in coordination with Saudi authorities and airlines, with regular updates on flight status, alternative routes and government instructions.

The columnist says the most urgent step is for the Bangladesh government to negotiate with Saudi authorities for extension of validity, keeping jobs open, or legal re-employment for workers whose visa or job term risks expiring, and to contact employers directly so that workers stuck in Bangladesh can return to their workplaces.

The columnist says newly recruited workers waiting to fly should get ticket rescheduling at no extra cost, refunds and alternative flights, and that any alternative employment arranged must be legal, verified and based on the worker's consent.

The columnist proposes that workers who borrowed to go abroad but cannot join their jobs be given temporary relief on loan repayment, rescheduled instalments and, depending on circumstances, financial help, coordinated by the government with financial institutions and the recruiting agencies concerned.

The columnist calls for a permanent emergency protection fund and a risk-based action plan for expatriates, deciding in advance how help is given, which agency does what and where the money comes from in case of war, pandemic, air-travel shutdown or sudden labour-market contraction.

The columnist says the labour welfare wing of embassies needs enough staff and working communication (hotline, updated instructions, complaint settlement, emergency legal aid), and proposes a trackable identification number for each affected worker's complaint showing the responsible officer, expected resolution time and progress, shared with the worker and family.

The columnist argues Bangladesh is over-dependent on a few labour markets, with limited skills and little preparation for alternative employment, and that government performance should be measured by how many workers kept their jobs, had visas extended, got unpaid wages and received emergency help, not by the number of meetings.

key_quote_bn: নতুন নিয়োগ নিয়ে অপেক্ষমাণ কর্মীদের জন্য বিনা অতিরিক্ত খরচে টিকিট পুনর্নির্ধারণ, অর্থ ফেরত এবং বিকল্প ফ্লাইটের ব্যবস্থা করতে হবে।

headline_en: Demand for Bangladeshi workers will rise in the post-war Middle East: expatriates' welfare minister in parliament
summary_en: Report of parliamentary question time on Thursday 3 September 2026. In written answers (delivered by State Minister Nurul Haque in the minister's absence), Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said the government expects demand for workers to rise for rebuilding infrastructure in Middle East countries damaged by the current war and is looking for new labour markets; that sending workers to Malaysia should open very soon after high-level visits; and gave last fiscal year's overseas employment figures by country. The rest of the article covers lightning deaths, earthquake volunteers and domestic labour courts.

facts.statement: The Bangladesh government told parliament it believes demand for workers will rise for rebuilding infrastructure in the Middle East countries damaged by the ongoing geopolitical unrest and war, and that it is taking steps to find new labour markets in the Middle East and elsewhere and create migration opportunities for Bangladeshi workers.
facts.source_in_article: Written answer of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury in parliament, delivered by State Minister Nurul Haque

facts.statement: The minister told parliament that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman recently visited Malaysia and that in late July (2026) the adviser and the minister of the Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry visited the country; as a result it is hoped the way to send Bangladeshi workers to Malaysia will be cleared very soon.

headline_en: Malaysia's labour market opened through bilateral meetings: Mahdi Amin
summary_en: At a press conference at the Bangladesh High Commission in Kuala Lumpur on Thursday 30 July 2026, the Prime Minister's adviser and spokesperson Mahdi Amin said Bangladesh and Malaysia had agreed in principle to reopen Malaysia's labour market to Bangladeshi workers in all sectors, with a target of workers starting to arrive from the last week of August 2026. He said Bangladesh asked that the first phase go through state-owned BOESL, that Malaysia will set the final number of recruiting agencies under the MoU valid until December 2026, and that those linked to the earlier syndicate and corruption would not be on the new list. He urged people to be patient, follow the correct process and beware of brokers.

facts.statement: Bangladesh and Malaysia agreed in principle to reopen Malaysia's labour market for Bangladeshi workers immediately, and reached a joint decision after talks with Malaysia's human resources minister to create work opportunities for Bangladeshi workers in all sectors.
facts.source_in_article: Mahdi Amin, adviser to the Prime Minister and spokesperson of the Prime Minister's Office, press conference at Bangladesh High Commission, Kuala Lumpur

facts.statement: A target was set by bilateral consensus for Bangladeshi workers to start arriving in Malaysia from the last week of August 2026; Mahdi Amin also said he hoped a number of workers would arrive and start work within about one month.
Bangladesh asked the Malaysian government to carry out the first phase of recruitment through the state-owned agency BOESL; BOESL is being given priority in the first phase.

Under the current Bangladesh-Malaysia memorandum of understanding, valid until December 2026, Malaysia will decide the final number of Bangladeshi recruiting agencies based on its own vetting and framework. A list of 423 recruiting agencies had been sent to Malaysia during the interim government; Bangladesh requested that the highest possible number of agencies be included.

Mahdi Amin said the Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry has already cancelled the licences of people linked to the previous 'fascist' government and involved in corruption and unethical activity, and that Bangladesh told Malaysia nobody who was part of the syndicate or involved in corruption should be on the new agency list; he said the Malaysian authorities would confirm this within a few days.

Technical-level work on reopening was to start very soon, led jointly by the Bangladesh High Commission in Malaysia and the Malaysian High Commission in Dhaka; Malaysia's Ministry of Human Resources and Bangladesh's expatriates' welfare ministry are jointly making the processes faster and more transparent. The Malaysian government was to give an update on its working method and formal procedures soon.

Mahdi Amin urged Bangladeshis to be patient and follow the correct process for going to Malaysia, and to be especially alert to fraud by brokers and dishonest rings; he said law enforcement and the administration in Bangladesh would be given instructions so nobody is harassed.
Mahdi Amin said instructions have been given to make the Bangladesh High Commission in Malaysia more people-friendly so that it becomes the main centre of trust for ordinary workers.

Mahdi Amin said the Malaysian labour market had been closed for several years mainly because of unethical practices and irregularities under the previous government; the interim government tried to restart it but it stayed closed because of various complications.

The stated priorities of the Bangladesh government for Malaysia are lowering migration cost, raising skills, reducing procedural complexity and sending skilled workers through a fully transparent process.

Labour and Employment and Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury and adviser Mahdi Amin were on a three-day state visit to Malaysia, held meetings over two days with Malaysia's human resources minister (named as R Ramanan / Datuk Seri R Ramanan), the ministry's secretary and assistant secretary; they had also met them about three months earlier. Bangladesh High Commissioner to Malaysia is Manjurul Karim Khan Chowdhury.

headline_en: Malaysia's labour market: how will a new door open with the old problems
summary_en: Opinion column (30 June 2026) by Dr Selim Reza of North South University after Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's visit to Malaysia. He says the visit did not immediately open the market, as media and some officials had suggested; its outcome was agreement in principle on transparent, fair, lower-cost recruitment, a Joint Working Group meeting and a decision to draft a new MoU. He reviews the history of suspensions, syndicate control, high costs and workers becoming irregular, and lists what a new MoU should contain.

facts.statement: During Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's visit to Malaysia, the talks with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim covered recruiting more Bangladeshi workers, quick opening of the labour market, legalising irregular workers and possible repatriation of detained Bangladeshis; both sides agreed recruitment must be transparent, fair and less costly so that middlemen's influence falls.
facts.source_in_article: Columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

facts.statement: The most significant outcome of the Bangladesh-Malaysia prime ministers' meeting was a decision to hold a Joint Working Group meeting and to draft a new memorandum of understanding (MoU) for safe and regular migration of Bangladeshi workers; the visit's main result was not an immediate opening of the market but agreement in principle.

Malaysia's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim publicly acknowledged that exploitation, lack of transparency and humanitarian concerns around the worker recruitment system are real and that both countries must act on them.

The columnist says that before the visit a large part of Bangladesh's media and some responsible government officials gave the impression that reopening of Malaysia's labour market was already decided and only a formal announcement remained, creating excess optimism among workers and families; in reality no immediate opening resulted.

Over the past decade the Malaysian market for Bangladeshi workers has been repeatedly closed or suspended, with allegations of control by a limited number of agencies and a syndicate; many workers spent several lakh taka to go and did not get the promised job, worked for low wages, became irregular or faced inhumane conditions.

The columnist explains the 'syndicate' mechanism: when recruitment to Malaysia is concentrated in a limited group, competition falls, cost rises and transparency shrinks; workers pay extra, often borrow, and spend their first few years abroad only repaying the debt.

Bangladeshi workers in Malaysia became irregular in several ways: some stayed after their visa expired, some were cheated by their employer, and some lost their job; a large share of them contribute to Malaysia's economy but lack legal protection.

The columnist says a new Bangladesh-Malaysia agreement should spell out minimum wage, working hours, safe housing, health care, a ban on confiscating passports, prevention of workplace discrimination and a quick, effective complaint mechanism, and should strengthen legal aid, consular services and the capacity of the Bangladesh mission and labour wing in Malaysia.

The columnist says the new MoU should make every recruitment step digital, set a maximum limit on recruitment cost, include joint monitoring and an independent complaint-resolution structure, and involve civil society, labour rights groups and research bodies.

Most Bangladeshi workers in Malaysia are still in unskilled or low-skilled work, which limits their income, while demand for skilled workers is rising in technology-based industry, construction, services and modern manufacturing; the columnist urges investment in technical, language and digital skills training.

key_quote_bn: অনেক শ্রমিক কয়েক লাখ টাকা খরচ করে গিয়ে প্রতিশ্রুত চাকরি পাননি, কম মজুরিতে কাজ করেছেন, অনিয়মিত হয়েছেন বা অমানবিক পরিস্থিতির শিকার হয়েছেন।

headline_en: Prime Minister calls for Malaysia's labour market to be opened quickly to Bangladeshis
summary_en: At a joint press conference with Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim at the Prime Minister's Office in Putrajaya at 11:30am local time on Monday 22 June 2026, Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman said he had asked Malaysia to recruit more Bangladeshi workers and open the labour market quickly, and raised legalisation of irregular workers and possible repatriation of detained Bangladeshis. He said both sides agreed recruitment must be transparent, fair and affordable. The rest of the article covers trade, investment, FTA talks, Rohingya, ASEAN and other bilateral matters.

facts.statement: Prime Minister Tarique Rahman said he asked Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim to consider recruiting more Bangladeshi workers and opening the labour market quickly; no opening was announced at the press conference.
facts.source_in_article: Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, joint press conference, Putrajaya

facts.statement: Tarique Rahman said he also raised with Anwar Ibrahim the legalisation of irregular (undocumented) Bangladeshi workers in Malaysia and the possible repatriation of detained Bangladeshis.
Bangladesh and Malaysia agreed that the worker recruitment process must be transparent, fair and affordable, so that the role of middlemen is reduced and workers' costs fall.

The Malaysia visit was Tarique Rahman's first foreign trip as prime minister (he took office in February 2026 after the 12 February 2026 election). Manpower and skills development were among the sectors discussed; a cultural MoU was signed and documents on counter-terrorism research cooperation and investment were exchanged; the two sides decided to advance talks on a Bangladesh-Malaysia free trade agreement.

Tarique Rahman said Bangladeshi workers, students, professionals and entrepreneurs in Malaysia act as an important bridge between the two countries. The Bangladesh delegation included Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman, Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque, and Mahdi Amin, adviser on education and overseas employment.

headline_en: Why this injustice to the remittance fighters?
summary_en: Opinion column (7 June 2026) by Mohiuddin Ahmed, a Canada-based analyst, arguing that Bangladesh's migrant workers are trapped by broker rings, excess migration cost, debt, skill gaps and lack of protection abroad, with women domestic workers worst off. He gives 2024 remittance and departure figures and sets out six proposals: wider government-run recruitment with a verifiable database, punishment for overcharging, modern district training centres, embassies as real shelters, employer background checks for women workers, and government migration loans.

facts.statement: Expatriates sent about USD 26.89 billion to Bangladesh in 2024, and in the same period more than about 1 million (10 lakh) Bangladeshis went abroad for employment.

The columnist says the government fixes a migration cost, and brokers and middlemen collect several times that amount; many families sell their homestead, borrow at high interest or beg from relatives, so the worker is in debt before setting foot abroad.

The columnist says many Bangladeshi workers go abroad without proper training, language learning or knowledge of the destination country's labour law, and so face low wages, risky work, breach of contract and exploitation, while demand for unskilled workers is falling.

Long-standing complaints from Bangladeshi workers abroad listed by the columnist: not being paid according to contract, passports being held, inhumane living conditions and abuse at work; embassies have labour welfare wings but there are long-standing complaints of not getting quick, effective help.

The columnist says many Bangladeshi women who go abroad as domestic workers face unpaid wages, confinement, physical and mental abuse and even sexual abuse, made worse by not knowing the language, having no safe way to complain, and depending on the employer's house as both workplace and shelter.

Proposal 1: widen government and semi-government recruitment models such as BOESL (printed 'বোয়েলস'), G2G and G2G Plus, and let workers verify job details, salary, cost, contract terms and visa authenticity directly through a government database.

Proposal 2: any agency or broker taking more than the government-fixed fee should face not only fines but licence cancellation, recovery of compensation and, if needed, criminal cases; every transaction should be digital so evidence of fraud cannot be destroyed.

Proposal 3: modernise district-level Technical Training Centres and make international-standard training and language learning compulsory in nursing, caregiving, driving, IT, electrical, plumbing, construction technology and hospitality.
Proposal 4: embassies should have a 24-hour hotline, emergency shelter, legal aid, translation help and a working system for receiving complaints against employers.

Proposal 5: make employer background checks compulsory before sending women workers, require strict bilateral agreements with countries where safety is not assured, suspend sending women workers in risky cases, and provide regular check-ins, an emergency helpline and safe shelters for women workers abroad.
Proposal 6: provide government migration loans on easy terms, tied directly to the approved migration cost, to replace brokers' loans.

key_quote_bn: সরকার একটি খরচ নির্ধারণ করে, আর দালাল ও মধ্যস্বত্বভোগীরা সাধারণ মানুষের অসহায়ত্বের সুযোগ নিয়ে তার কয়েক গুণ বেশি টাকা আদায় করে।

headline_en: Returnee workers tell their stories of getting back on their feet
summary_en: At a BRAC event in a Dhaka hotel on Thursday 14 May 2026, organised by the EU- and BRAC-supported Prottasha project for reintegrating returnees, returned migrants from Cyprus and Italy described rebuilding their lives with project support. State Minister Md Nurul Haque said government support for returnees is perfunctory and that BDT 13,500 for rehabilitation is too little, and said the more than 3,000 recruiting agencies will be vetted and graded, with over 600 possibly not surviving.

facts.statement: The Prottasha project, run with support from the European Union and BRAC, works on rehabilitating returned migrants; in its first phase the International Organization for Migration (IOM) worked with BRAC, and in the current second phase IOM gives policy support. Returnees named in the article got help from it to start a small business (a scooter for tea delivery; a grocery shop).
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report of BRAC event

facts.statement: Besides BRAC, a government project called RAISE (রেইজ) works on rehabilitating returned workers.

State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare Md Nurul Haque said the government's support for returnees is perfunctory and that BDT 13,500 (sare 13 hajar taka) for rehabilitation is very little and must be increased.

State Minister Md Nurul Haque said there are currently more than 3,000 recruiting agencies in Bangladesh; they will be vetted and graded, and more than 600 agencies may not survive. Qualified agencies will be encouraged and those involved in fraud should face strict punishment.

State Minister Md Nurul Haque said the government has taken a strict position against human trafficking and irregular migration, that the trend of going abroad by sea must be stopped, and that the government will act against those pushing young people towards death on sea routes.

Selina (printed as both Selina Begum and Selina Hossain) of Tangail went to Cyprus through a broker with her husband's help, could not last there and returned empty-handed; after return her husband pressed her to repay the money and she did not leave the house for a month because of social stigma against women who go abroad.
facts.source_in_article: Returnee Selina, speaking at BRAC event

facts.statement: Sohel Rana of Tangail went to Romania through a broker, was well for 2 years, and when his contract ended went to Italy by an irregular route after several attempts; he found no work there, became helpless and returned to Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: Returnee Sohel Rana, speaking at BRAC event

facts.statement: BRAC chairperson Hossain Zillur Rahman said government and non-government bodies must work together on safe migration and returnee welfare; Md Shariful Islam, head of the BRAC Migration Programme, presented the Prottasha project's work. Other speakers included the ministry secretary Md Mokhtar Ahmed and Wage Earners' Welfare Board director general Md Asaduzzaman.

headline_en: We are alert so that workers going to Malaysia do not fall into a ring: expatriates' welfare adviser
summary_en: At a press conference on Wednesday 20 August 2025 on the ministry's one year of work, Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Adviser Asif Nazrul said the government is trying to stop an agency syndicate in Malaysia recruitment and to get all agencies a chance, but that the agreement signed by the previous government lets Malaysia choose the agencies. He listed the year's actions: agreements with Japan, Korea, Italy and European countries, a Japan cell, a deal to send 8,000 workers who missed Malaysia in 2024 through BOESL, payments to 188 returnees from the UAE, multiple-entry visas in Malaysia, regularisation in Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Oman, an airport expatriate lounge, and replacing the private 'Ami Probashi' app with a government platform issuing BMET emigration clearance fully online.

facts.statement: Adviser Asif Nazrul said the previous government signed the agreement with Malaysia for sending workers, and the agreement itself says Malaysia will select the agencies; the agreement cannot be changed by force. Bangladesh has told Malaysia in every meeting that all recruiting agencies should get the chance, as in other countries.
facts.source_in_article: Asif Nazrul, Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Adviser, press conference at the ministry

facts.statement: Asif Nazrul said that when recruitment is given to specific agencies, workers are cheated, migration cost rises and many kinds of corruption occur; the government is alert so workers going to Malaysia do not fall into any syndicate or corruption ring.

Amin Nur, described by the article as a Bangladeshi-origin Malaysian citizen and the main figure of the Malaysia worker recruitment ring, works with the Malaysian government, according to Adviser Asif Nazrul, who said Bangladesh has nothing to discuss with him and talks directly with the Malaysian government.

An agreement was signed with Malaysia to send 8,000 workers who could not go last year (2024) because the labour market closed; state-owned BOESL (Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited) has taken up sending them at nominal cost.
Multiple-entry visas have been introduced for Bangladeshi workers in Malaysia for the first time.

A 'Japan cell' has been formed to send more than 5 lakh (500,000) workers to Japan in the next 5 years; several agreements have been signed with Japan, an agreement with Korea, and agreements with several European countries, with emphasis on sending skilled workers to Europe and Japan because demand for unskilled workers is falling.
A memorandum of understanding on migration was signed between Bangladesh and Italy for sending workers.

188 workers who returned from the United Arab Emirates (expatriates who took part in the student-people's movement) each received BDT 50,000 from the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry, BDT 94 lakh in total, plus BDT 13,500 each as counselling and financial incentive; those wanting to go abroad again are to be sent to Brunei, and local rehabilitation has also been started.

An agreement with Saudi Arabia to expand safe and legal migration, the first of its kind, was due to be signed in September 2025; a joint task force has been formed to solve the problems of Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia.

Steps have been taken to regularise irregular Bangladeshi women workers in Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Oman; a process is under way to legalise women workers in Jordan and more than one lakh (100,000) undocumented workers in Oman.
An 'Expatriate Lounge and Waiting Lounge' (Probashi Lounge) has been set up at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, with hygienic food at a 30 percent discount.

The interim government shut the private app 'Ami Probashi' and built an integrated government online platform for overseas employment; BMET (Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training) now issues emigration clearance directly and 100 percent online on the government's own platform, which the adviser said lets workers get clearance in less time and at lower cost.

headline_en: BAIRA demands quick opening of all labour markets including Malaysia
summary_en: On Thursday 24 April 2025, recruiting agency owners under the banner 'general members of BAIRA' formed a human chain in front of Probashi Kalyan Bhaban in Eskaton, Dhaka, demanding that Malaysia and all closed labour markets be opened quickly. They said 13 countries accepted Malaysia's conditions and kept their markets open, and blamed a vested group raising 'false' trafficking and money-laundering allegations for the delay. They gave a memorandum to the adviser.

facts.statement: As of 24 April 2025 the Malaysian government had not yet opened its labour market to Bangladeshi workers, according to members of BAIRA (Bangladesh Association of International Recruiting Agencies).
facts.source_in_article: BAIRA members at human chain, Eskaton, Dhaka

facts.statement: BAIRA members said 13 countries accepted the Malaysian government's conditions and kept their labour markets open, while Bangladesh lags behind and is losing Malaysia's market of 12 lakh (1.2 million) workers.

BAIRA members claimed a vested group is obstructing reopening by raising what they called false allegations of human trafficking and money laundering in Malaysia recruitment and questioning the MoU signed between the two countries and the Joint Working Committee's decisions.

BAIRA members estimate that if the Malaysian market reopens, at least 2 lakh workers a year, 10 lakh over five years, could be sent, earning Bangladesh at least USD 500 crore (5 billion) in remittance a year.
After the human chain a memorandum was handed to the manpower export and overseas employment adviser demanding that Malaysia and all closed labour markets be opened for low-cost, safe migration.

headline_en: Libya to Italy: why the desperate journey on the 'road of death'
summary_en: Explainer (16 February 2025) on why and how Bangladeshis travel irregularly from Libya to Italy by boat. It describes the route (Dhaka to Dubai by air, then Turkey or Egypt, then Libya, then boats from Zuwara and Tajoura to Sicily), the price of BDT 15 to 25 lakh, the three stages ending in an asylum claim, and how people die or end up in Libyan or Tunisian jails. It gives figures from Frontex, IOM, InfoMigrants, Italian ministries and the Bangladesh ambassador in Libya, says legal labour migration to Italy is currently closed, and quotes experts.

facts.statement: The usual irregular route to Italy: traffickers and their brokers fly migrants from Bangladesh to Dubai, send them on to Turkey or Egypt, then to Libya, and from Libya by sea to Italy. The price stated is BDT 15 lakh to a maximum of 25 lakh.

Costs quoted for the irregular Libya-Italy journey differ by source in the same article: BDT 15 to 25 lakh (reporter), BDT 20-25 lakh (Syed Saiful Haque, chairman of WARBE Development Foundation), and BDT 15-20 lakh (Dr Md Jalal Uddin Sikder, North South University). A related headline in the article mentions a BDT 16 lakh 'body contract' Dhaka to Italy.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo; Syed Saiful Haque; Dr Jalal Uddin Sikder

facts.statement: In Libya brokers put migrants into a group and give them a few days' training in steering by compass at sea; boats leave for Italy from the Zuwara (জোয়ারা) and Tajoura (তাজোরা) coasts of Libya. The trained migrants themselves steer the boat; the brokers do not go along and nobody takes responsibility once the boat leaves.

Boats from Libya aim for the Italian island of Sicily. Because a few days' training is not enough to navigate, boats often drift by mistake to Malta, where those caught by law enforcement are sent back to Libya; others are sent by coast guards to ports in Libya or Tunisia, where they end up in prison; others drift and drown.

Second stage: on reaching Sicily the migrants surrender to the Italian navy patrolling the sea and are then sent to detention ('jail'). Third stage: they claim political asylum; Italian police and human rights organisations give those rescued from the sea the chance to apply.
If the asylum claim is approved, the irregular migrant begins living in Italy; if it is not approved, Italian police give the person about a week to leave Italy and return to Bangladesh.

The crossing is made in small or medium boats, sometimes inflatable boats, packed tight; many die of suffocation below deck or of hypothermia on the long sea journey, and fellow passengers put the bodies into the sea.

According to InfoMigrants as cited, more than 4,000 Bangladeshis went to Italy irregularly in 2024 and more than 700 people died in boat sinkings and other ways. The same article also cites InfoMigrants that 49,691 people reached Italy by sea in January-October 2024, of whom 12,702 were Bangladeshi (20 percent, the largest group); the two Bangladeshi figures do not agree.
In 2023, 3,760 migrants went missing or died trying to enter European countries by sea; several hundred of them are thought to be Bangladeshi.

23 bodies were recovered on Libya's east coast; the Bangladesh embassy in Tripoli told the foreign ministry that the bodies were washed at Ajdadiya (আজদাদিয়া) hospital in the Brega area, and a Bangladeshi who took part thought from the appearance of the decomposed bodies that all were Bangladeshi.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh embassy in Tripoli, to the foreign ministry

facts.statement: 150,652 Bangladeshis were living in Italy with valid papers as of 1 January 2022, the highest among EU countries, according to a report of Italy's Ministry of Labour and Social Policies published in July 2023; the number of undocumented Bangladeshis in Italy is more than 50,000 (Italian interior ministry figure cited).
facts.source_in_article: Italian Ministry of Labour and Social Policies report (July 2023); Italian interior ministry

facts.statement: Districts from which most people go to Italy include Shariatpur, Madaripur, Gopalganj, Faridpur, Cumilla, Sylhet and Chandpur; boat migrants are mostly from Shariatpur, Madaripur, Faridpur, Chandpur, Munshiganj, Brahmanbaria, Cumilla and Sunamganj. Many who reach Italy later move on to Greece, Spain or France.

Frontex's annual report says 8,667 Bangladeshis entered European countries irregularly in 2024: 7,574 via the Central Mediterranean, 604 via the Eastern Mediterranean and 'the remaining' 437 via the Western Balkans (the three parts as printed add up to 8,615, not 8,667).
facts.source_in_article: Frontex annual report, cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: IOM's annual report says the Libyan coast guard intercepted 21,700 irregular migrants in the Mediterranean in 2024, including 1,500 women and 700 minors. InfoMigrants says the Turkish coast guard detained 55,467 irregular migrants off Turkey's coast in 2024.
About 10,000 Bangladeshis living irregularly in Italy are getting a chance to become legal by correcting their passport information; the opportunity lasts until 30 April 2025.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo (citing Italian interior ministry data in the same paragraph)

facts.statement: Sending workers to Italy through the legal process is currently closed; Italy wants the more than 50,000 Bangladeshis staying there irregularly to be sent back, and taking new workers will stay closed until then.

410 Bangladeshis are currently in Libyan prisons after being caught crossing the Mediterranean towards Italy. More than 21,000 Bangladeshis work in Libya as migrants, 80 percent without valid papers. 4,200 Bangladeshis were sent home from Libya last year (2024).
facts.source_in_article: Major General Abul Hasnat Muhammad Khairul Bashar, Bangladesh ambassador to Libya

facts.statement: The Bangladesh ambassador to Libya said the Bangladesh government has a list of human traffickers and brokers and that these 'mafia' are very influential; WARBE chairman Syed Saiful Haque said the government, law enforcement and the embassies in Libya and Italy hold the lists, offenders are arrested after media reports but get out on bail within days and resume trafficking.
facts.source_in_article: Ambassador Abul Hasnat Muhammad Khairul Bashar; Syed Saiful Haque, WARBE Development Foundation

facts.statement: BRAC research says a large share of those who go from Bangladesh to Europe through brokers have no work at home; others are from rural farming families, construction workers (especially plumbers and electricians), and people who worked in hotels, restaurants and grocery shops.
facts.source_in_article: BRAC research, cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Professor C R Abrar, executive director of RMMRU, said legal opportunities for workers to go to Italy and many European countries have shrunk, pushing people to brokers, and the government should urgently negotiate bilaterally to increase legal labour intake and prepare a long-term anti-trafficking action plan; he said he sees no such effort.
facts.source_in_article: Professor C R Abrar (Dr Chowdhury Rafiqul Abrar), RMMRU

facts.statement: Google Maps distance from Libya to Italy is given as 1,778 km.
facts.source_in_article: Google Maps, cited by Prothom Alo

headline_en: Malaysia's labour market: what can be done to stop syndicates, corruption and irregularities
summary_en: Opinion column (9 October 2024) by Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-e-Jannat of North South University, written after Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's visit to Bangladesh. It says migration to Malaysia is very costly and controlled by syndicates in both countries, that the B2B, G2G and G-Plus models all failed, and proposes alternatives: a Philippines-style government placement and migration insurance, IOM IRIS ethical-recruitment certification, a government e-wallet for all fees, union-level one-stop centres, a public-private partnership for direct hiring, demand-led training with a job portal, and social media information.

facts.statement: Thousands of Bangladeshi workers go to Malaysia each year, mainly for construction, agriculture and manufacturing; the cost of going is described as sky-high, and after arrival many workers do not get the promised pay and work.
facts.source_in_article: Columnists Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-e-Jannat, North South University

facts.statement: The columnists say powerful syndicates exist in both Malaysia and Bangladesh that control the recruitment process, which creates the opening for cheating Bangladeshi workers and forces them to bear high costs.

Bangladesh has tried business-to-business (B2B), government-to-government (G2G) and government-plus-business (G-Plus-B2B) models for sending workers to Malaysia; the columnists say none has proved effective so far.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim recently visited Bangladesh (before 9 October 2024), which the columnists say created new prospects for the Malaysian labour market.

Proposal (Philippines model): BMET (Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training) should work directly with Malaysian employers to place workers without middlemen, and set up a migration insurance/protection fund under BMET covering medical, legal and rehabilitation help.

Proposal (ethical recruitment): introduce compulsory certification modelled on IOM's IRIS (International Recruitment Integrity System), with regular audits of legal fee limits and worker protection; only certified agencies could send workers to Malaysia, and a BMET-IOM digital platform would let workers see which agencies are certified and their costs.

Proposal (digital migration wallet): all migration fees should be paid through a government-controlled e-wallet that BMET and the Malaysian government can both monitor, leaving no room for extra or hidden fees.

Proposal: BMET should open union-level 'one-stop service' centres for job applications, visa processing, document processing and training, so workers need not travel far or depend on brokers to reach recruiting agencies.

Proposal (PPP model): a partnership between the Malaysian government and BMET in which Malaysian companies hire directly from Bangladesh, encouraged by tax breaks or other incentives, with joint regular audits of hiring companies to prevent hidden fees.

Proposal (training): BMET's technical training centres should train to skills identified with Malaysian employers, issue internationally recognised certificates, offer government support and loans for training cost, and run a job portal with profiles of trained workers for employers to hire from directly; BMET should also publish job and fee information on social media and hold online seminars on recruitment and legal rights.

key_quote_bn: মালয়েশিয়ায় পৌঁছানোর পর অনেক শ্রমিক প্রতিশ্রুত বেতন ও কাজ না পেয়ে নানান প্রতারণার শিকার হন।

headline_en: Lack of jobs at home, young people desperate to go abroad
summary_en: Economy feature (19 August 2024) on young Bangladeshis leaving for work because decent jobs are scarce at home. It gives BMET departure figures for 2019 to early 2024, Wage Earners' Welfare Board figures on forced returnees with out-passes in 2023, Saudi remittance trends, BRAC-sourced figures on irregular travel to Europe via the Mediterranean and its cost, and the number who went abroad for higher study in 2023. It includes one aspiring migrant's case and comments from SANEM and BRAC.

facts.statement: BMET figures: a record of more than 13 lakh (1.3 million) workers went abroad in 2023, on average about 150 per hour; more than 11 lakh 35 thousand went in 2022; 322,207 went in January-April 2024.
facts.source_in_article: BMET (Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training), cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: BMET figures: about 7 lakh workers went abroad in 2019, only about 2 lakh 17 thousand in 2020 (Covid), and more than 6 lakh 17 thousand in 2021.

Government statistics: 20 to 22 lakh young people enter the labour market each year; 12 to 13 lakh get jobs inside the country, about 85 percent of them in wage-based informal work (about 3 lakh decent jobs a year); 8 to 9 lakh go abroad each year, and over 10 lakh a year went in 2022 and 2023. One third of all new jobs for Bangladeshis each year are abroad.
facts.source_in_article: Government statistics, cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Bangladesh ranks sixth among countries by size of population living abroad and seventh by remittance received. Low-educated youths mainly go to Middle East countries (Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Oman).

Workers who return destitute, after being detained by law enforcement abroad, or otherwise forced, are given an out-pass (a valid travel permit) by the Bangladesh embassy to return home; only returnees with out-passes are counted, so the true number of returnees is unknown.
Wage Earners' Welfare Board data: 86,621 expatriates returned to Bangladesh on out-passes in 2023, of whom 83,719 were men and 2,902 women.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board, cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: About 17 lakh (1.7 million) workers went to Saudi Arabia in the last three years, yet remittance from Saudi Arabia fell from more than about USD 550 crore a year three years ago to about USD 350 crore a year now, which the article reads as workers not earning well.

106,598 Bangladeshis crossed the Mediterranean to Europe between 2009 and May 2024, according to sources connected with BRAC, which supports people forced to return after irregular attempts to reach Europe.
facts.source_in_article: BRAC-related sources, cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Bangladeshis detained or identified while trying to reach Europe irregularly on eight identified routes: 2,254 in 2019, 5,426 in 2020, 9,208 in 2021, 17,101 in 2022 and 15,506 in 2023; the Mediterranean route is the most used and Bangladeshis are the largest group attempting it.
facts.source_in_article: BRAC sources, cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Young Bangladeshis trying to reach Europe irregularly are aged 31 to 35 and have to spend BDT 15-20 lakh; most are from Dhaka, Sylhet, Sunamganj, Shariatpur and Madaripur districts. A large share of those who get in apply for political asylum in France, the United Kingdom, Greece and other countries.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo ('it is learned'; BRAC sources)

facts.statement: Selim Raihan, executive director of SANEM, said many frustrated youths sell land and borrow to go to Middle East countries, live in miserable conditions and complain of not getting fair wages for their labour, while others attempt the very hard route to Europe.
52,799 Bangladeshis went abroad for higher education in 2023.

Mohammad Ripon of Chauddagram, Cumilla, who holds a driving licence and a passport, sold some family land and a few months before August 2024 gave 'some money' (amount not stated) to a broker for a job abroad; he was still waiting. He currently earns BDT 15,000 a month driving a rental car in Dhaka's airport area.

headline_en: Sending workers to Malaysia will start late next week: expatriates' welfare minister in parliament
summary_en: On Sunday 15 November 2026 Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury told parliament that the list of medical test centres for Malaysia-bound workers would be published on Monday 16 November and that workers should be able to go from late the following week to the end of the month. He said the cost has been fixed at BDT 154,000 and anyone charging more will face strict action; an MP said people are currently paying BDT 7 to 8 lakh. The article adds that Malaysia has listed BOESL and 25 private agencies, plus 312 more agencies allowed to work.

facts.statement: The Bangladesh government has fixed the cost of sending a worker to Malaysia at BDT 154,000 (1 lakh 54 thousand taka), reduced from earlier levels; the minister said strict action will be taken against anyone who collects more or commits irregularities outside the government-set system.
facts.source_in_article: Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, in parliament

facts.statement: MP Atiqur Rahman Mujahid said in parliament that sending a worker to Malaysia currently costs up to BDT 7 to 8 lakh, and asked whether a separate parliamentary committee could monitor whether workers can go at the fixed BDT 154,000.
facts.source_in_article: MP Atiqur Rahman Mujahid, supplementary question in parliament

facts.statement: The list of medical (health test) centres for workers going to Malaysia was to be published on Monday 16 November 2026.
facts.source_in_article: Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, in parliament on 15 November 2026

facts.statement: The minister said he hoped sending workers to Malaysia would begin by the end of the following week, with workers able to go between late that week and the end of November 2026.
facts.source_in_article: Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, in parliament

facts.statement: Malaysian authorities have listed Bangladesh's only state recruiting agency BOESL (Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited) and 25 private agencies as 'processing agency or service agency', and have allowed a further 312 recruiting agencies to work alongside them.
A listed agency for Malaysia may find employers on its own initiative, collect its own demand letters, select its own workers in Bangladesh and carry out their recruitment according to the rules.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman visited Malaysia in June 2026 on his first foreign trip, where reopening the labour market was discussed; the agency listing followed from that. A related headline in the article says testing has begun of workers interested in going to DHL in Malaysia at no cost.

headline_en: Expatriates will be able to enter Saudi Arabia even if their iqama has expired: expatriates' welfare minister
summary_en: On Monday 26 October 2026, at a discussion at the BIAM Foundation auditorium in Dhaka, Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said Saudi-based Bangladeshis stuck in Bangladesh by flight disruption whose iqama has expired will be allowed to enter Saudi Arabia, being automatically included in the Saudi system once they can travel. The disruption follows Houthi attacks on Saudi airports; 144 flights to and from Bangladesh have been affected. He also told agencies not to charge BDT 7-8 lakh where BDT 3 lakh is enough, and agencies asked for the Takamol test to be simplified and fees cut.

facts.statement: Saudi-based Bangladeshi workers stuck in Bangladesh because of flight disruption whose iqama (work/residence permit) has expired will get the chance to enter Saudi Arabia: the minister said that when the war situation improves and workers can travel, they will be automatically included in the Saudi system and will get permission to enter.
facts.source_in_article: Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury; ministry press release, 26 October 2026

facts.statement: Flight disruption arose after attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports by the Iran-backed armed group the Houthis; so far 144 flights on direct and transit routes with Bangladesh have been disrupted, so many workers cannot return on time after leave and their iqama may expire.

The minister said migration cost must come down: where it is possible to go for BDT 3 lakh, taking BDT 7-8 lakh is improper; recruiting agencies were urged to stop collecting extra money from workers.
facts.source_in_article: Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, via ministry press release

facts.statement: The minister said work is under way to introduce modern technology at BMET (Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training) to simplify the departure process and quickly verify visa validity, and that an open e-mail service for resolving any complaint is to be launched and publicised (no address printed).
facts.source_in_article: Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, via ministry press release

facts.statement: State Minister Md Nurul Haque drew the Saudi government's attention to bringing Bangladeshis imprisoned in Saudi Arabia under a special pardon next Ramadan; this was a request, not an announced decision.
Saudi ambassador Abdullah Zafer H bin Abiyah said Bangladeshi workers are the largest group living in Saudi Arabia after its own citizens.
Recruiting agency representatives at the meeting demanded simplification of the Takamol (তাকামুল) test process, lower fees, and resolution of BMET manpower-related complications.

The minister stressed that workers must properly obey the laws of the country they go to; the meeting was about expanding migration of skilled workers in strict compliance with Saudi Arabia's applicable rules.

headline_en: Two Bangladeshis executed in Saudi Arabia: are expatriates only money machines?
summary_en: Opinion column (17 October 2026) by Asif Bin Ali on the execution in Saudi Arabia of two Bangladeshis accused of immoral acts in a Makkah mosque, of which the Bangladesh consulate says it had no formal advance notice. He raises consular access under the Vienna Convention, and cites figures on Saudi executions, women migrant workers' bodies returned, legal aid given through missions, legal-aid agreements and safe homes, plus the case of a woman domestic worker missing for years.

facts.statement: Two Bangladeshis were executed in Saudi Arabia on an accusation of immoral activity in a mosque in Makkah; the Saudi interior ministry statement said they were sentenced to death under ta'zir (discretionary punishment). Their occupation and status in Saudi Arabia are not known, and the full court judgment has not been published.
facts.source_in_article: Columnist Asif Bin Ali, citing Prothom Alo reporting and the Saudi interior ministry statement

facts.statement: The Bangladesh consulate said it was not formally informed of anything before the executions were carried out. Two Bangladeshis assisted as interpreters during the trial, but it is not known whether the accused had lawyers, appealed, or had the chance to contact the consulate.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh consulate, per Prothom Alo report cited by the columnist

facts.statement: The columnist states that under Article 36 of the 1963 Vienna Convention on Consular Relations a foreign national who is arrested must be told of the right to consular contact; if he requests, his country's consulate must be notified, and consular officers can contact him and help arrange legal representation.
facts.source_in_article: Columnist Asif Bin Ali (who says he is not a law student)

facts.statement: Amnesty International counts at least 356 executions in Saudi Arabia in 2025, including foreign nationals, and has raised serious concern especially about the death penalty for drug-related offences.
facts.source_in_article: Amnesty International, cited by the columnist

facts.statement: The expatriates' welfare minister said in April 2026 that about 30 lakh (3 million) Bangladeshis are working in Saudi Arabia.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' welfare minister, cited by the columnist

summary_en: The Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry said on Friday (about 28 August 2026) that Malaysia has agreed in principle to take Bangladeshi workers again. At the government's special request Malaysia agreed in principle to take 10,000 workers at zero cost, the first batch to go through state-owned BOESL on special chartered flights. Malaysia directly selected 25 Bangladeshi agencies, allowed 312 more as 'associate recruitment agencies', and will start with 16 medical centres. The ministry told people not to make any payment, take medical tests or hand over passports until it issues a notice.

facts.statement: Malaysia has agreed in principle to take workers from Bangladesh again, and sending workers is to start as soon as possible, the Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry said.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry press release

facts.statement: At the Bangladesh government's special request, Malaysia agreed in principle to take 10,000 workers at no cost to the workers, with no expenses of any kind including airfare.

The market is to restart with the first batch of the 10,000 zero-cost workers being sent to Malaysia through the state-owned BOESL (Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited) on special chartered flights.

Under the memorandum of understanding signed in 2022, the Malaysian government alone has the responsibility of selecting the Bangladeshi recruiting agencies that send workers to Malaysia; the MoU runs until 31 December 2026, which the ministry says is why Bangladesh cannot easily change Malaysia's conditions. The ministry hopes a new MoU after that date will protect Bangladesh's interest in agency approval.

Malaysia directly selected 25 Bangladeshi recruiting agencies, all from the list of 423 agencies prepared by the previous interim government, and is allowing a further 312 agencies to send workers as 'Associate Recruitment Agency'; the sole state agency BOESL can also work in the process. Agency names are not printed.

The agencies were selected by a high-level joint committee of Malaysia's Ministry of Human Resources, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of Home Affairs, anti-corruption commission and law enforcement; the Bangladesh ministry says the Bangladesh government had no involvement at all in the selection.

Bangladesh requested Malaysia to exclude from the agencies those who benefited under the previous government and were involved in the syndicate and to let the remaining agencies send workers; the ministry says Malaysia gave this opportunity on special consideration.

Medical centres: Bangladesh asked to change the currently approved medical centres; a joint team from Malaysia's health, human resources and home ministries visited Bangladesh and inspected each centre. Malaysia decided to start with 16 medical centres remaining on its existing approved list after 'controversial' centres were dropped at Bangladesh's request; after the market opens, a team from the three Malaysian ministries will come to prepare a new list under a new policy.

The ministry said the specific process for sending workers to Malaysia is still being finalised and will be announced in due time, and urged everyone not to make any payment, undergo any medical test or hand over a passport until the ministry issues a notice or instruction.

The ministry's release says the Malaysian labour market had closed because of corruption, misrule, syndicate and irregularities under the previous government, and that confusion being spread about the reopening is unwarranted.

headline_en: Initiative being taken to bring the whole process of sending workers abroad online: expatriates' welfare minister
summary_en: At a roundtable on safe migration and reintegration of returnees at the Prothom Alo office in Karwan Bazar, Dhaka, on Tuesday 18 August 2026 (co-organised by BRAC Migration Programme and Prothom Alo with EU support), Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said the whole process of sending workers abroad will be made online. He described plans: a month-long campaign against irregular migration in several districts, employer-verified training (already used for 6,000 drivers for the UAE), third-party and courier delivery of embassy services, a 'Probashi Card', a higher education loan limit at Probashi Kallyan Bank, and strengthening 104 technical training centres.

facts.statement: The minister said an initiative is being taken to make the whole process of sending workers abroad online, with more transparency in information on the legality of recruiting agencies and overseas demand for workers.
facts.source_in_article: Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, roundtable at Prothom Alo office

facts.statement: The minister said the routes of rings sending people abroad irregularly are being identified for action, and that an intensive one-month publicity campaign is planned in several districts from Sunamganj and Habiganj to Madaripur.

A new method: when a country asks for workers with a specific skill, the employer's representative or trainer comes to Bangladesh to verify the training and recruits only after being satisfied. This method has been introduced for the United Arab Emirates taking 6,000 drivers from Bangladesh; the minister said it reduces the scope for middlemen.

The minister said workers are often sent without the skill the foreign employer asked for, for example a person who does not know the work being sent where plumbers or electricians were demanded, causing trouble for both worker and employer.

The minister said the government is considering delivering some embassy/consulate services through third parties, and is thinking about delivering passports and other documents to expatriates' homes by post or courier, because expatriates now travel long distances to embassies at a cost of time and money. These are under consideration, not in place.

A 'Probashi Card' for expatriates is planned and is to be finalised as part of the government's 180-day programme; it may give expatriates priority in government services including land and sub-registry offices, and special health-care benefits; an MoU between two ministries has been signed on this.
The minister said there is a plan to raise the limit of the education loan for expatriates' children through Probashi Kallyan Bank from BDT 3 lakh to BDT 10 lakh.

Bangladesh has 104 technical training centres which the minister said need skilled trainers and proper infrastructure, not just buildings; Qatar has shown interest in providing trainers and funding to Bangladesh's technical training centres.

The minister said madrasa students, already ahead in Arabic, can be made ready for the Middle East labour market in a short time, and that such an initiative in three madrasas in his constituency gave positive results.

The minister said many people sell land and assets to try to go abroad irregularly, and when they get into trouble their families are left destitute and deaths occur; he called for awareness campaigns through media, social media, mosques, temples and churches.

headline_en: The way to send workers to Malaysia will be cleared soon: expatriates' welfare minister
summary_en: In parliamentary question time on Tuesday 23 June 2026, the day after Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's bilateral meeting in Malaysia, Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said the government is working to open Malaysia's labour market and hopes the way will be cleared very soon, and that it is trying to get undocumented Bangladeshis in Malaysia legalised. He said no workers are sent to Malaysia by the government itself, and gave remittance figures for fiscal year 2024-25. The rest of the article is about food stocks.

facts.statement: The minister told parliament the government is working to open Malaysia's labour market and hopes the way to send Bangladeshi workers will be cleared very soon; he said there was positive progress after the Prime Minister's recent Malaysia visit. As of this date the market was not yet open.
facts.source_in_article: Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, answer to MP Reza Ahmed in parliament

facts.statement: The minister said the government is making efforts to legalise Bangladeshi workers who are staying in Malaysia irregularly or are in various difficulties.

The minister said no workers are sent by the government itself to Malaysia, which he called the second largest labour market for Bangladeshi workers; workers can go to Malaysia or any other country through government-approved recruiting agencies.
Bangladesh received a total of USD 3,032 crore (30.32 billion) in remittance in fiscal year 2024-25, the highest share, USD 426 crore, coming from Saudi Arabia.
facts.source_in_article: Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, answer to MP Selina Sultana

named_actors.what_the_article_says: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister; answered questions on Malaysia and remittances in parliament.
